query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the identity of the X element controls the selective oxidation kinetics such that an Al substitution promotes the formation of a coherent, slow-growing, protective oxide layer (via the formation of adherent Al2O3 mixed with Cr2O3) above 900 °C, whereas Si or Mn additions lead to oxide scales that grow faster and are prone to cracking or spalling.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys manufactured as single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solutions, with X being either Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Systematically alloy the base CrFeCoNi composition with  an addition of  appropriate concentrations of either Si, Mn, or Al, ensuring comparable processing to achieve similar grain structures and phase distributions.
generation.conditions: Expose the alloys to high-temperature (above 900 °C) isothermal oxidation tests in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere (e.g., air with controlled humidity) for prolonged durations (up to 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The composition and microstructural integrity of the oxide scale at the alloy surface (in particular, the presence and distribution of Al2O3 and Cr2O3 versus other less adherent oxides).
generation.mechanism: The mechanism involves selective oxidation kinetics where Al, due to its lower diffusion rate and favorable thermodynamics, forms a slow-growing, adherent alumina layer that mixes with chromia to accommodate stresses and match the thermal expansion of the substrate. In contrast, Si or Mn do not form oxide scales with similar protective characteristics, leading to higher oxygen fluxes, increased growth stresses, and eventual scale cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al as X will exhibit a thinner, cohesive, and slowly growing oxide scale with fewer cracks or spallation events, while those with Si or Mn will develop thicker, less coherent oxide scales that are more prone to cracking and spallation above 900 °C.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the CrFeCoNi alloy without a reactive X addition (or with a non-optimizing X) that does not form a stable, protective oxide layer under high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Valid under high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidation or corrosive environments, over prolonged exposure (e.g., up to 100 hours), and for alloys processed to similar single- or multiphase solid-solution states.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences in oxide growth rates and mechanical adherence between the different X modifications are uncertain and may also depend on minor processing variations and local compositional heterogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of CrFeCoNi alloys, each modified with  a fixed concentration of either Al, Si, or Mn as the X element via identical processing routes. Subject parallel samples of each alloy to isothermal oxidation at 950 °C in air (or a controlled corrosive atmosphere) for durations up to 100 hours. Post-exposure, characterize the oxide scale using X-ray diffraction (for phase identification), scanning electron microscopy (for scale morphology and thickness), and adhesion/scratch tests to assess coherence.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate (using cross-sectional SEM)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (via XRD)
Scale adherence and presence of spallation or cracking (using scratch testing and optical microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxide growth rate and improved scale coherence (i.e., a thinner, more adherent oxide with fewer cracks) compared with the Si- and Mn-containing alloys, or if Si or Mn alloys unexpectedly exhibit protective, coherent oxide scales similar to or superior to the Al alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

A careful observation of the time-dependent concentration change plots for varying Al to Cr ratios shows an interesting difference between Al and Cr oxides with the rest of the oxides. The fluctuation of the concentration of thermodynamically unstable oxide (Fe, Co, and Ni oxides) is higher than thermodynamically stable oxides (Al and Cr oxides), making the lines of Figure 5d–f appear thicker than Figure 5b,c. Similar observations can be made for all the oxide concentration plots, as well. As Fe, Co, and Ni oxides are thermodynamically unstable, the formation and dissociation occur more frequently in these oxides as compared to Al and Cr oxides.
